As Editor-in-Chief **Mags Corliss** notes, this persistent fog acts as a quiet blanket that slows pedestrian movement, muffles city signals, and shifts human connection into warm interior gathering spots [1, 2]. references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C108 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ The morning fog that Noah Tan's reporting caught this week — Marc Allie adjusting the thermostat a third time in his Laurel kitchen, Tyrie Groin pulling her coat tighter on the way to work — feels like the right metaphor for what this city is living through in Y2C108. Something is muffling the signal. Money is moving, projects are in motion, teams are on the field, and yet everywhere you turn, Oakland is straining to hear itself think.

The fog and gray were all over the week, by the way. Noah Tan's pieces have Colin Soria blowing on his hands outside the laundromat, and the people he talked to called the weather "neutral" and "deliberate." I'll take the dull gray days as a small mercy. They gave the city a week to slow down and notice things. On the field, Simon Leary wrote the most careful column of the week about the A's. They are 1-0 and have won two straight, and there's a role change on the team that nobody has explained. I can't square 1-0 with two straight wins either, and I won't pretend to. Simon's restraint is right. A record is a beam, not a forecast. And over in Rockridge, Nia Rook found the neighborhood still lit up after Otis Redd's night on UNDOCKED, a 143-credit swing that has people arguing about who holds the edge and for how long. Rockridge, sitting at the top of the school table, can afford the entertainment. I won't begrudge anyone a good night.

What I'm watching next week: whether anyone in city government responds to the accountability vacuum Luis documented, because that piece ends mid-sentence — and the silence where a name should be is the loudest thing in this paper. I'm also watching the Stabilization Fund's next disbursement checkpoint, and whether Baylight's construction pace starts pulling workers from the same West Oakland neighborhoods the fund is supposed to protect. Those two stories are converging. I want to know if anyone in city hall sees it yet.

============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic Marc Allie adjusted the thermostat in his Laurel kitchen for the third time that morning, his hands lingering on the dial as the fog pressed against the windows. Outside, the neighborhood felt cloaked, the usual morning bustle reduced to muted footsteps and the occasional soft hum of a car engine. Inside, the table was cluttered with textbooks and half-finished assignments—homework the kids couldn’t seem to focus on.

"The fog in Oakland? It’s like a quiet blanket that slows everything down," Allie said, pouring himself a cup of coffee. "You feel it in your bones, especially early mornings when I’m heading out for my shift. It’s not just the chill—it’s the way it makes the neighborhood feel smaller, more intimate. Like the world’s holding its breath." Across town, Tyrie Groin pulled her coat tighter as she walked to her retail job. The fog lingered, draping familiar streets in a muted gray. "It’s introspective, you know?" she said. "Makes you appreciate the warmth of family and the comfort of routine even more."

============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Weight of Neutral By Noah Tan Colin Soria blew on his hands outside the Temescal laundromat, watching his breath hang in the air just long enough to be seen before vanishing. The security guard’s usual post-shift ritual—picking up takeout, maybe stopping by the bus shelter to chat with neighbors—had been pared down to just this: a quick errand, then home. "It’s not the kind of weather that stops you in your tracks," he said, nodding at the overcast sky. "Just that dull, gray blanket that makes everything feel a little slower." His rounds this week had been quieter, his head cold lingering like the fog from yesterday. Even the laundromat’s usual murmur of conversation had dimmed to the occasional rustle of turning pages.

And Maria Keen's piece reminds us who is arriving. Temescal has 311 kids, eight more than last cycle. It has 2,106 working adults, fifty-one more, and 294 seniors, seven more. Nobody is leaving those numbers. Yet the one program of organized care on Maria's block is the Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry, which has been standing since C83. Omar Lingio loves the fog that settles on his store. Marc Allie and Jackson Sift have both heard, secondhand, about a Temescal Holiday Market. Neither could say where or when. I'd like to know too, and I hope someone with the details calls us. A growing neighborhood with the lowest school index on the table and one pantry holding the line is carrying a lot on a thin frame.

Omar Lingio will tell you it's the fog. "It's moments like those that remind me why I love Temescal so much," he said. "I was just standing there, watching the fog roll in, and it felt like the whole neighborhood was wrapped in this quiet, peaceful blanket. The rest of the city might have been sunny and bustling, but here, it was like time stood still. I felt grateful to be a part of this community, to have my store here and be able to experience days like that." He's not wrong that the weather plays favorites with this block. It settles here when the rest of the city stays clear, like it's got an address to keep.

Rick Walker is at his desk before the first bell, red pen in hand, grading spelling tests in a Fruitvale classroom that still smells like floor wax. He's got a stack of papers and a former line cook's habit of working fast under pressure. When I ask what's on his mind outside the classroom, he doesn't talk about his students. He talks about a transit project. "I've heard folks around here talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II," he says, red pen still moving, "but honestly, it feels like the council's been dragging their feet. People want accountability, but it's hard to tell who's really stepping up to make things happen."

============================================================ By Luis Navarro | Bay Tribune Civic The Same Empty Lot, Four Times Rick Walker stands at the chain-link fence at the corner lot two blocks from his school, waiting for the crossing guard to wave the line of kids through. It's the same lot it was last year. He teaches K-8 in Fruitvale, cooked line before that, and he's got maybe four minutes before the bell before he has to be back inside. "Honestly, I hear teachers and parents at school talking about how the city keeps promising things for Fruitvale but nothing ever moves forward," he tells me, one eye on a kid untying his shoe mid-crosswalk. "We see the same empty lots year after year, and nobody ever explains why."

That's one voice, one neighborhood. It stops being local when you hear it again in Temescal. Melton Neilon has flour on his forearms at whatever hour bakers call morning, folding dough on a bench that's seen this motion ten thousand times. He's not talking about bread. "I've heard folks talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II, and it feels like there's a lot of uncertainty about who's really driving it forward," he says. "It's frustrating when you don't know who's accountable or what's being done to make it happen."

I don't have an explanation for him. There isn't one on the record. Three miles north, Melton Neilon is bagging sourdough loaves at the Temescal farmers market table, flour on his forearms, half-listening to the vendor next to him complain about parking. He's not from Fruitvale. He doesn't need to be to have heard about it. "I've heard folks at the farmers market talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub delays," Neilon says, "but honestly, I'm not sure who's supposed to be steering it forward. It feels like everyone's waiting for someone else to take charge."

Same words, almost. Different oven, different neighborhood, same blank space where a name should be. Cross the city to Rockridge and the pattern holds. Elio Perez, working the floor on a slow shift, says it plain: "I've heard people talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II, but it feels like the council's been dragging their feet. It's frustrating because we need that kind of investment in our neighborhoods." His coworker Depak Ying, same restaurant, same shift, echoes it back with a different word choice but the identical shape of complaint: "I've heard people talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II visioning, and it feels like there's a lot of confusion about who's really in charge and what's being done. It's frustrating because it's such an important project for the community."

That's the sentence that stuck with me. Not the complaint — the shrug inside it. Nobody in this cycle's record names who's steering. Over in Rockridge, servers Elio Perez and Depak Ying are working the same lunch rush at the same diner, six tables apart, and somehow talking about the same lot in Fruitvale neither of them has a stake in. "Honestly, I hear folks at the diner grumbling about how nothing ever moves forward with the Fruitvale plans," Perez says between orders, "but nobody seems to know who's actually holding the reins or why it's stuck."

Ying, wiping down a table Perez just cleared, doesn't disagree. "I've heard people talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub delays, and it feels like no one's stepping up to take responsibility — it's frustrating because we need that progress." Four people. Three neighborhoods. Zero names. Here's what the record gives me and what it doesn't. What it gives me: the city signal this cycle flagged a civic gap — accountability, or the absence of it, tied to Fruitvale. And it gives me this: no civic initiative on the books this cycle addresses that signal. Not a placeholder, not a stalled line item. Nothing pointed at it at all.

Luis Navarro found the same gap wearing different clothes over in Fruitvale. He sat with a teacher named Rick Walker, grading spelling tests with a red pen still moving, who told him the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II feels like the council dragging its feet. Then Luis found a baker in Temescal with flour on his forearms saying almost the same words. Then two servers in Rockridge. Four people, three neighborhoods, zero names attached to the project. What Luis is describing isn't just public confusion — it's the sound a city makes when accountability has been designed out of a process. Nobody in those conversations claimed they'd asked and been refused an answer. They're not describing a wall. They're describing a void. That's harder to fix, because voids don't fight back.

Four people. Three neighborhoods. Zero names. Nobody in these four conversations can tell you who owns this file. Not the baker, not the teacher, not either server. That's not an accusation — none of them claim to have asked and been refused. They're describing a rumor mill with no source at the center of it, a project that everyone's heard about and nobody can point to. I went looking for what fills that gap this cycle. There isn't a civic initiative on the books addressing the signal these four residents are circling. Not a task force, not a working group, not a name attached to Phase II that any of them, or the record I have, can produce.

That question of who's responsible followed me east. Luis Navarro spent his week with the same empty lot in Fruitvale, and what struck him was how far the frustration traveled. Rick Walker, who teaches K-8 nearby, said it plainly: the same empty lots year after year and nobody explains why. But it was Melton Neilon, bagging sourdough at a Temescal farmers market table, and two Rockridge servers, Elio Perez and Depak Ying, who made Luis's point. People with no stake in Fruitvale know the transit hub is stalled, and none of them can say who is steering it. Luis found nothing on the books this cycle aimed at that gap. I don't have a name to give Rick either, and that bothers me more than the delay does.

What it doesn't give me is a name. Not an office, not a person, not a duty assigned to anyone who could pick up a phone and explain the lot. I don't have a request on file. I don't have a response, or a refusal, or a date stamped on either. There isn't one to report — which is different from saying nobody's ever going to answer. It just means nobody's on record answering yet. So I'm left with what four residents in three different neighborhoods noticed without prompting each other: a stalled thing with no fingerprints on it. That's not proof of wrongdoing. It's proof that the story of who's responsible hasn't been told to the people standing at the fence.

What makes it sharper is Trevor Shimizu's reporting on the trains. Ridership jumped nearly 30 percent across the system, with 99,582 boardings. Fruitvale Station alone logged 10,414, up 3,756. Eleanor Rivera at 12th Street, which took in 23,848 riders, says her team "just adapts." Jerald Jensen, the janitor there, put it more honestly: trash cans overflowing by noon and no time to catch his breath between rushes. Joel Wren, the AC Transit mechanic, credits the crews keeping buses moving. Part of the surge was a game day and a pair of big events at Lake Merritt, so I wouldn't read it as a permanent shift. Still, people are pouring through Fruitvale Station while the hub beside it sits stuck. On-time performance improved, to 85 percent at 12th Street and 81 percent at Fruitvale. The workers are holding the system together. I'd like to see the planners do the same for the lot.

The station isn’t alone. Across Oakland, ridership has jumped nearly 30% this cycle, with 99,582 boardings logged across eight stations and ten corridors. Coliseum Station saw 9,724 riders, a spike of 4,859 from the last cycle, while Fruitvale Station recorded 10,414 boardings, up 3,756. Even MacArthur Station, quieter by comparison, saw a 24% increase, with 12,030 riders passing through its gates. The reasons aren’t hard to spot. Downtown hosted a game day, while Lake Merritt saw two major events. The Baylight District’s ongoing construction planning has also redirected traffic, funneling commuters toward 12th St. Joel Wren, an AC Transit mechanic who works near the station, has noticed the uptick firsthand. “You know, I’ve been seeing more folks hopping on the buses lately—especially down at 12th Street,” Wren says. “It’s good to see people out and about, trusting the system again. But what really gets me is the crew keeping those buses running. Those mechanics and drivers? They’re the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, especially with all these extra riders.”

On-time performance has improved at most stations, with 12th St hitting an 85% on-time rate, up four points from the last cycle. Fruitvale Station, despite its own surge, managed an 81% rate, up three points. Even Coliseum Station, often a laggard, saw its rate climb to 83%, up five points. The question now is how long this surge will last—and whether the system can sustain it. ============================================================ By Trevor Shimizu | Bay Tribune Civic Ridership Surge at 12th St Oakland City Center Tests Transit Systems At 12th St Oakland City Center, the fares click louder and more often. Eleanor Rivera, a BART station manager, has felt the surge in her bones—23,848 riders this cycle, up 5,472 from the last. “It’s not just numbers,” Rivera says. “It’s people adjusting their routines, and us adjusting right along with them. The team just... adapts. No big announcements, just everyone doing their part to keep things moving smoothly.”

Jerald Jensen, a janitor at the station, sees the surge in the wear and tear. “More coffee spills to mop up, more trash cans overflowing by noon,” Jensen says. “Used to be you could catch your breath between rushes, but now? It’s constant. Folks pouring in for work, for games, for whatever’s happening downtown.” Coen Cartier, a transit operator, echoes the sentiment. “It’s been busy, but it feels good to know we’re helping people get where they need to go,” Cartier says. “The team’s been working hard to keep things running smoothly, and it’s paying off.”

The two civic stories sit next to each other this week like a matched pair of warnings. In one, money is flowing but residents can't trace where it lands. In the other, a project is talked about citywide but nobody can name who owns it. Oakland has a transparency problem that isn't about secrecy — it's about structure. The systems for connecting decisions to people don't appear to exist, or if they do, they're not functioning at street level. Meanwhile, Jordan Velez spent time at the Anthropic construction site on Baylight Avenue, where the old rail yard is giving way to glass and steel. Kelvon Ochoa, an AI safety researcher, noticed more familiar faces at the coffee shops. Brianna Lee, a preservation carpenter with Baylight Construction Authority, described the energy as the district coming alive. And Tariq Jello, adjusting his hardhat, observed with the precision of someone who's watched neighborhoods change before: the coffee shops are busier, the plumbing problems are the same. Velez didn't oversell this, and I'm glad — because the question he left open, about who the district will truly serve as it grows, is the question that connects directly to what Carmen and Luis are reporting. Growth without accountability infrastructure doesn't stabilize anything. It just moves the instability around.

Here is what I'm watching next week. First, whether the Stabilization Fund shows up where Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark can see it, in a rent kept in check or a household that stays. Second, whether anyone claims the Fruitvale hub, and whether the crowds at that station get an answer for the lot beside it. Third, whether Temescal gets a second program, a clearer school story, or at minimum a date and a street for that holiday market. And fourth, whether the A's can explain their own role change. I'll be listening for names this week. The city has plenty of complaints. What it's short on is somebody saying "that one's mine."

============================================================ By Angela Reyes | Bay Tribune Civic The Finish Line That Isn't Lo Thoop stands in the hallway outside the creative writing classroom in Temescal, watching students filter past at 3 p.m. on a Wednesday. The school quality index reads 6.8—the lowest on the city table. Across the street, Rockridge sits at 8.87. But Lo isn't thinking about rankings right now. Lo is thinking about the gap between what the diploma says and what comes after. "You know, living here in Temescal, I've seen kids graduate—they walk across that stage, families cheering—but then there's this quiet worry afterward," Lo says. "Are they really ready for what's next? It's like we're celebrating the finish line, but the race isn't over. I teach creative writing, and I see it in their essays—bright ideas, but sometimes they're missing the tools to build on them. It's not just about getting them out the door; it's about making sure they're equipped to walk through the next one."

The numbers seem to tell one story. Eighty-five percent of Temescal students graduate. But only fifty-seven percent test college-ready. That gap—twenty-eight percentage points—sits in the silence between ceremony and consequence. Patricia Nolan, who taught in Temescal for decades before retiring, speaks from the weight of that silence. "After teaching for so many years, I've seen kids walk across that graduation stage who can barely write a proper paragraph," Patricia says. "The numbers might say 85% graduate, but half of them aren't ready for what comes next. It's not just about passing classes—it's about whether these kids can actually think critically when they leave here. We celebrate the diploma, but we're not always honest about what it really means."

In the student zone, the ranking feels distant. Jun Leu, sitting on a bench near the gym, doesn't track the index. "I don't really think about graduation rates or college stuff yet. At school, we just do our work and go home. Some kids talk about college, but most just wanna play basketball or hang out after class," Jun says. "My cousin Ira says high school is harder than middle school though." Salma Navarro nods along the same current. "I don't really think about the numbers. At school, everyone's just trying to get through the day. Some teachers really push us, but others just let things slide. My brother Hector says high school was like that too—you could graduate easy, but actually being ready for what's next? That's different."

The Oakland Unified School District employs 5,201 people citywide and is growing. Temescal's school receives $11,500 in per-student funding—less than Rockridge's $15,000. The city's teacher quality score here sits at 6.96. The question that hangs in the hallway, in the essays, in the families' quiet worry: Is this a resource problem, a culture problem, or something harder to name and fix? By Simon Leary | Bay Tribune Sports The Load That Doesn't Bend By Simon Leary Vladimir Gonzalez stands at the edge of the batting cage, glove tucked under his arm, watching the arc of balls meeting bats. The right fielder’s stance is loose, familiar—a player who knows both his place in the lineup and the quiet weight of maintaining it. Around him, the rhythm of swings and catches hums with the steadiness of a team that has won five straight, a team that wakes up each morning to find its record at 3-0 for the cycle.

The sentiment is admirable, but the Phillies’ pitching staff won’t care about heart when Horn steps to the plate. His struggles are amplified by the success of his teammates. Eric Taveras is hitting .359 with four home runs. Vladimir Gonzalez has matched Taveras' power output while batting .286. Ernesto Quintero, often hitting behind Horn, has three homers and a .324 average. In a lineup that has otherwise thrived, Horn’s slump stands out like a sore thumb. "Danny Horn’s been grinding, and I respect that," manager Deacon Seymour said. "The numbers don’t tell the whole story—he’s a guy who shows up every day, puts in the work, and keeps his head in the game. Right now, he’s not finding the gaps, but I’ve seen him turn it around before."

The A’s have managed to win despite Horn’s struggles, but the margin for error becomes razor-thin in the World Series. Game 1 starter Arturo Ramos, who carries a 1.93 ERA into tonight’s contest, knows the stakes. "Numbers don’t always tell the whole story—he’s got the kind of at-bats that wear pitchers down," Ramos said of Horn. "We’re not worried. When it clicks for him, it’s gonna be big." The question isn’t just whether Horn can turn it around—it’s whether the A’s can survive another series if he doesn’t. With Philadelphia’s rotation looking formidable on paper, Oakland may not have the luxury of carrying a slumping star. For a team chasing its seventh ring, the margin for error has never been smaller.

This is not momentum. Momentum implies a force gathering itself, a thing that could be spent. What the A’s have built is something more tectonic: a structure where roles shift seamlessly beneath the surface, where each piece bears just enough load to keep the whole upright. "You see it in how guys prepare every day," Gonzalez says later, peeling tape from his wrists. "How nobody gets too high or too low. We just keep grinding." His words are less about effort than about trust—the kind that lets a team redistribute its weight without buckling. Across the clubhouse, veterans like Vinnie Keane nod at the same idea. "It’s not just about the wins," he offers. "It’s about knowing your part and playing it right, even when the spotlight’s not on you."

Here is the unseen architecture: a roster where every player adjusts without protest, where legends like Darrin Davis remember a time when such flexibility was rare. "You know, when you're in the middle of a streak like this, it's not about any one guy carrying the load," Davis reflects. "It's about each of us finding new ways to contribute when the moment calls for it. I've seen pitchers turning into leaders in the clubhouse, rookies stepping up like seasoned vets, and guys like me adjusting how we play to fit what the team needs that day. That's the secret - everyone being willing to shift roles without ego."
